abstract: A fundamental question of developmental biology is pattern formation, or how cells with specific gene expression end up in specific locations in the body to form tissues, organs, and, overall functional anatomy. abstract: The vast collection of human-specific traits—such as our unique morphology, cognition, behavior, and diseases—has long been attributed to gene expression divergence between us and our closest living relatives, chimpanzees. title: Synthetic torpor in the rat protects the heart from ischaemia-reperfusion injury
abstract: During times of environmental stress, many animals enter torpor: a reversible protective physiological state typically characterised by reductions in core temperature, heart rate, and oxygen consumption. Species that naturally enter this hypothermic and hypometabolic state are tolerant of ischaemia-reperfusion injury. Consequently, there is a growing interest in utilising aspects of torpor for clinical applications such as protection from stroke or myocardial infarction. It is currently unknown, however, whether a torpor-like state is protective in animals that do not naturally enter torpor. Using viral vector-mediated chemogenetic activation of the medial preoptic area of the hypothalamus, we induced synthetic torpor in the rat, a species that does not naturally enter torpor. title: Cholinergic blockade reveals a role for human hippocampal theta in memory encoding but not retrieval
abstract: Cholinergic dysfunction is a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease and other memory disorders. Yet, the neurophysiological mechanisms linking cholinergic signaling to memory remain poorly understood. In this study, we administered scopolamine, a muscarinic cholinergic antagonist, to neurosurgical patients with intracranial electrodes as they performed an associative recognition memory task. abstract: Ewing sarcoma (EwS) is a fusion-driven malignancy, peaking in adolescence. Although EwS tumors are driven uniquely by EWS::FLI1 and related fusions, patient outcomes vary greatly. title: Engineering ATP import in yeast uncovers a synthetic route to extend cellular lifespan
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction and declining ATP production are common features of aging, yet whether ATP availability itself directly regulates cellular lifespan is unclear. However, the causal relationship between cellular ATP homeostasis and aging has not been established. Here, we developed a synthetic system to manipulate intracellular ATP independently of endogenous energy production by expressing a plasma membrane-targeted nucleotide transporter, NTT1, from the intracellular parasite Encephalitozoon cuniculi in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. NTT1 expression depleted intracellular ATP in the absence of extracellular ATP, whereas ATP supplementation produced robust NTT1-dependent ATP uptake, and increased intracellular ATP abundance. abstract:

The origin of paired fins was a major event in early vertebrate history that fueled the adaptive radiation of the gnathostome clade. title: Towards improving the safety of medication use in pregnancy
abstract:
by Jennifer Jardine, Suzanne de Bruijn, on behalf of the PLOS Medicine staff editors

Pregnant people are historically excluded from clinical trials, meaning safety information regarding medication use during pregnancy is scarce. Despite efforts to change this, inclusion of pregnant people in trials is complicated. Observational studies may represent the most effective and timely method to close this evidence gap, but guidelines to optimise their value are needed. In this Editorial, Jennifer Jardine and Suzanne de Bruijn highlight the evidence gap on the safety of medication use during pregnancy, and outline how observational studies may present an effective and timely method to close this gap.

abstract:
by Adwoa Kumiwa Asare Afrane, Marilyn Naana Ahun

Paediatric HIV and tuberculosis care in Africa pays little attention to children’s caregivers, although their mental health matters for child outcomes and family wellbeing. We argue that new continental and Ghanaian policy commitments offer a rare chance to make the family the unit of care. In this Perspective, Adwoa Afrane and Marilyn Ahun outline why greater attention is needed to the mental health of caregivers for children with HIV and/or tuberculosis, and discuss how recent policy commitments in Africa, including the Accra declaration, offer a rare opportunity for meaningful action.
